claim: Megaselia abdita shared a last common ancestor with Drosophila melanogaster about 150 million years ago.
source: M. abdita shared a last common ancestor with D. melanogaster about 150 million years ago (Wiegmann et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wiegmann et al., 2011.

claim: Overall embryonic development of M. abdita and D. melanogaster is conserved and comparable.
source: While overall embryonic development of M. abdita and D. melanogaster is conserved and comparable (Wotton et al., 2014), the two species differ in their extraembryonic development (Rafiqi et al., 2008; Wotton et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wotton et al., 2014.

claim: M. abdita and D. melanogaster differ in their extraembryonic development.
source: While overall embryonic development of M. abdita and D. melanogaster is conserved and comparable (Wotton et al., 2014), the two species differ in their extraembryonic development (Rafiqi et al., 2008; Wotton et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rafiqi et al., 2008 and Wotton et al., 2014.

claim: In D. melanogaster, the amnioserosa is set up as a single extraembryonic epithelium by expression of the Hox3 transcription factor Zerknüllt (Zen).
source: In D. melanogaster, the amnioserosa is set up as a single extraembryonic epithelium by expression of the Hox3 transcription factor Zerknüllt (Zen), which is controlled by peak levels of BMP signaling along the dorsal midline of the blastoderm embryo (Gavin-Smyth and Ferguson, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gavin-Smyth and Ferguson, 2014.

claim: Zen expression in D. melanogaster is controlled by peak levels of BMP signaling along the dorsal midline of the blastoderm embryo.
source: In D. melanogaster, the amnioserosa is set up as a single extraembryonic epithelium by expression of the Hox3 transcription factor Zerknüllt (Zen), which is controlled by peak levels of BMP signaling along the dorsal midline of the blastoderm embryo (Gavin-Smyth and Ferguson, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gavin-Smyth and Ferguson, 2014.

claim: M. abdita develops two distinct extraembryonic tissues, the serosa and the amnion.
source: In contrast to D. melanogaster, M. abdita develops two distinct extraembryonic tissues, the serosa and, bordering it, the amnion (Kwan et al., 2016; Rafiqi et al., 2008; Rafiqi et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kwan et al., 2016; Rafiqi et al., 2008; and Rafiqi et al., 2012.

claim: In the M. abdita blastoderm embryo, expression of the zen orthologue defines the serosa anlage along the dorsal midline.
source: In the M. abdita blastoderm embryo, expression of the zen orthologue defines the serosa anlage along the dorsal midline (Rafiqi et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rafiqi et al., 2008.

claim: A narrow domain void of both zen and general embryonic patterning genes was identified as putative amnion anlage in M. abdita.
source: Adjacent to this zen-defined serosa anlage, but within the range of dorsal BMP signaling, a narrow domain void of both zen and general embryonic patterning genes was identified as putative amnion anlage (Figure 1A; (Kwan et al., 2016; Rafiqi et al., 2012)).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kwan et al., 2016 and Rafiqi et al., 2012, and by Figure 1A.

claim: Cells of the serosa and amnion anlage undergo synchronous cell shape changes in M. abdita.
source: Cells of the serosa and amnion anlage undergo synchronous cell shape changes and eventually differentiate into squamous epithelia.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text as a description of observed cellular behavior.

claim: Cells of the serosa and amnion anlage eventually differentiate into squamous epithelia in M. abdita.
source: Cells of the serosa and amnion anlage undergo synchronous cell shape changes and eventually differentiate into squamous epithelia.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text as a description of observed cellular behavior.

claim: The serosa separates from the adjacent amnion in M. abdita.
source: The serosa then separates from the adjacent amnion, spreads freely, and continuously increases its cell size until it closes as perfect envelope on the ventral side of the egg (Rafiqi et al., 2008; Rafiqi et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rafiqi et al., 2008 and Rafiqi et al., 2010.

claim: The serosa spreads freely after separating from the amnion in M. abdita.
source: The serosa then separates from the adjacent amnion, spreads freely, and continuously increases its cell size until it closes as perfect envelope on the ventral side of the egg (Rafiqi et al., 2008; Rafiqi et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rafiqi et al., 2008 and Rafiqi et al., 2010.

claim: The serosa continuously increases its cell size until it closes as perfect envelope on the ventral side of the egg in M. abdita.
source: The serosa then separates from the adjacent amnion, spreads freely, and continuously increases its cell size until it closes as perfect envelope on the ventral side of the egg (Rafiqi et al., 2008; Rafiqi et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rafiqi et al., 2008 and Rafiqi et al., 2010.

claim: M. abdita has been previously identified as key organism to understand the evolutionary origin of the amnioserosa as a single, non-spreading extraembryonic epithelium.
source: Because the serosa in M. abdita has retained the ancestral ability to expand and envelope the embryo proper, the species has been previously identified as key organism to understand the evolutionary origin of the amnioserosa as a single, non-spreading extraembryonic epithelium (Hallgrímsson et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hallgrímsson et al., 2012.

claim: The serosa in M. abdita has retained the ancestral ability to expand and envelope the embryo proper.
source: Because the serosa in M. abdita has retained the ancestral ability to expand and envelope the embryo proper, the species has been previously identified as key organism to understand the evolutionary origin of the amnioserosa as a single, non-spreading extraembryonic epithelium (Hallgrímsson et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is stated as a reason for M. abdita being identified as a key organism, supported by citation to Hallgrímsson et al., 2012.

claim: The serosa developed from a dorsal anlage that was about six to seven cells wide.
source: The serosa developed from a dorsal anlage that was about six to seven cells wide (Figure 1B,B').
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 1B,B'.

claim: Serosa cells did not divide during development.
source: These cells did not divide, increased in cell surface area (Figure 1C,C'), and eventually spread over the adjacent tissue (Figure 1D,D').
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figures 1C,C' and 1D,D'.

claim: Serosa cells increased in cell surface area during development.
source: These cells did not divide, increased in cell surface area (Figure 1C,C'), and eventually spread over the adjacent tissue (Figure 1D,D').
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 1C,C'.

claim: Serosa cells eventually spread over the adjacent tissue.
source: These cells did not divide, increased in cell surface area (Figure 1C,C'), and eventually spread over the adjacent tissue (Figure 1D,D').
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 1D,D'.

claim: The width of the inferred serosa domain perfectly coincided with gene expression of the known serosa key regulator Zerknüllt (Zen).
source: The width of the inferred serosa domain perfectly coincided with gene expression of the known serosa key regulator, the homeodomain transcription factor Zerknüllt (Zen), while the observed cell dynamics matched serosa behavior as previously inferred from fixed specimen (Rafiqi et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with gene expression data and citation to Rafiqi et al., 2008.

claim: The observed cell dynamics matched serosa behavior as previously inferred from fixed specimen.
source: The width of the inferred serosa domain perfectly coincided with gene expression of the known serosa key regulator, the homeodomain transcription factor Zerknüllt (Zen), while the observed cell dynamics matched serosa behavior as previously inferred from fixed specimen (Rafiqi et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Rafiqi et al., 2008.

claim: A single row of cells directly adjacent to the serosa anlage was identified as presumptive amnion.
source: Directly adjacent to the unambiguously identified serosa anlage, we identified a single row of cells (Figure 1B,B''), which increased in apical cell area (Figure 1C,C'') but eventually did not become part of the spreading serosa (Figure 1D,D'').
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figures 1B,B'', 1C,C'', and 1D,D''.

claim: Presumptive amnion cells increased in apical cell area.
source: Directly adjacent to the unambiguously identified serosa anlage, we identified a single row of cells (Figure 1B,B''), which increased in apical cell area (Figure 1C,C'') but eventually did not become part of the spreading serosa (Figure 1D,D'').
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 1C,C''.

claim: Presumptive amnion cells did not become part of the spreading serosa.
source: Directly adjacent to the unambiguously identified serosa anlage, we identified a single row of cells (Figure 1B,B''), which increased in apical cell area (Figure 1C,C'') but eventually did not become part of the spreading serosa (Figure 1D,D'').
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 1D,D''.

claim: Presumptive amnion cells did not divide.
source: These cells did not divide (Figure 1E), and, consistent with patterning information in the early blastoderm embryo (Figure 1A; (Kwan et al., 2016; Rafiqi et al., 2012)), formed the presumptive amnion.
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Cells next to the amnion increased in apical cell area temporarily.
source: Next to the amnion, cells increased in apical cell area temporarily (Figure 1B,B''',C,C''') but eventually divided and decreased in size (Figure 1D,D''',E), suggesting differentiation into ectodermal cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figures 1B,B''', 1C,C'''.

claim: Cells next to the amnion eventually divided and decreased in size, suggesting differentiation into ectodermal cells.
source: Next to the amnion, cells increased in apical cell area temporarily (Figure 1B,B''',C,C''') but eventually divided and decreased in size (Figure 1D,D''',E), suggesting differentiation into ectodermal cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figures 1D,D''', 1E and involves inference about cell fate.

claim: Serosa cells increased in surface area up to 10-fold after germband extension.
source: The overall analyses of surface cell area at later stages of development, that is after germband extension, indicated a substantial increase in surface area for serosa cells (up to 10-fold), a still notable increase for presumptive amnion cells (about 2-fold), and a slight reduction of cell surface area in the ectoderm (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Presumptive amnion cells increased in surface area about 2-fold after germband extension.
source: The overall analyses of surface cell area at later stages of development, that is after germband extension, indicated a substantial increase in surface area for serosa cells (up to 10-fold), a still notable increase for presumptive amnion cells (about 2-fold), and a slight reduction of cell surface area in the ectoderm (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Ectodermal cells showed a slight reduction of cell surface area after germband extension.
source: The overall analyses of surface cell area at later stages of development, that is after germband extension, indicated a substantial increase in surface area for serosa cells (up to 10-fold), a still notable increase for presumptive amnion cells (about 2-fold), and a slight reduction of cell surface area in the ectoderm (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The M. abdita amnion consists of a lateral tissue which is essentially one cell wide and a cap at the posterior end of the germband.
source: Thus following development of the presumptive amnion through consecutive stages of development, our results suggested that the M. abdita amnion consisted of a lateral tissue, which was essentially one cell wide, and a cap at the posterior end of the germband that closed over the ventral side of the embryo (which, because of the extended germband, faced the dorsal side of the egg; Figure 2A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figures 2A-D.

claim: During germband extension and up until the onset of germband retraction, cells of the presumptive lateral amnion had a rather smooth outline and appeared to be folded over the ectoderm.
source: During germband extension and up until the onset of germband retraction, cells of the presumptive lateral amnion had a rather smooth outline and appeared to be folded over the ectoderm; with the onset of germband retraction, these cells then seemed to reside more over the yolk and developed notable protrusions towards the dorsal midline of the embryo (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figures 2C,D.

claim: With the onset of germband retraction, lateral amnion cells seemed to reside more over the yolk and developed notable protrusions towards the dorsal midline of the embryo.
source: During germband extension and up until the onset of germband retraction, cells of the presumptive lateral amnion had a rather smooth outline and appeared to be folded over the ectoderm; with the onset of germband retraction, these cells then seemed to reside more over the yolk and developed notable protrusions towards the dorsal midline of the embryo (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figures 2C,D.

claim: Amnion cells initially remained in contact with the F-actin front and appeared to get dragged over the adjacent ectoderm by the steadily expanding serosa.
source: In these renderings, we then analyzed the behavior of lateral amnion cells relative to the serosa by using enrichment of F-actin (revealed by our Lifeact reporter) between the two cell types as local hallmark. Following this hallmark, amnion cells initially remained in contact with the F-actin front and appeared to get dragged over the adjacent ectoderm by the steadily expanding serosa (Figure 2H,H').
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figures 2H,H'.

claim: After having been passed over by the serosa, amnion cells stopped moving towards the ventral midline.
source: After having been passed over by the serosa, amnion cells stopped moving towards the ventral midline.
evidence: The claim is stated as an observation from the analysis.

claim: The F-actin front continued to expand evenly towards the ventral midline together with the leading edge of the serosa after amnion cells stopped moving.
source: By contrast, the F-actin front continued to expand evenly towards the ventral midline together with the leading edge of the serosa (Figure 2H''), indicating that serosa leading edge and lateral amnion had disjoined.
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 2H''.

claim: Serosa leading edge and lateral amnion had disjoined after amnion cells stopped moving towards the ventral midline.
source: By contrast, the F-actin front continued to expand evenly towards the ventral midline together with the leading edge of the serosa (Figure 2H''), indicating that serosa leading edge and lateral amnion had disjoined.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that the F-actin front continued with the serosa but not the amnion, as shown in Figure 2H''.

claim: Following disjunction, the presumptive amnion cells seemed to be turned with their lateral side towards the basal membrane of the serosa.
source: Following this disjunction, the presumptive amnion cells seemed to be turned with their lateral side towards the basal membrane of the serosa (Figure 2B,H; Figure 2—video1).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figures 2B,H and Figure 2—video1.

claim: During germband retraction, amnion cells no longer appeared folded over the adjacent ectoderm but rather over the yolk sac.
source: This orientation was reversed during germband retraction, when amnion cells no longer appeared folded over the adjacent ectoderm but rather over the yolk sac (Figure 2D,I–I'''; Figure 2—video2).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figures 2D,I–I''' and Figure 2—video2.

claim: First signs of serosa tissue expansion were identified at about 35 min after onset of germband extension.
source: Accordingly, we identified first signs of tissue expansion at about 35 min after onset of germband extension (Figure 3A; Figure 3—video1; Figure 3—video2).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 3A and videos.

claim: The serosa approached the equator at the poles at about 150 min after onset of germband extension.
source: The serosa approached the equator at the poles at about 150 min (Figure 3B) and passed it 15 min later; ventral fusion along the midline was then completed at about 240 min (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The serosa passed the equator at the poles 15 min after approaching it.
source: The serosa approached the equator at the poles at about 150 min (Figure 3B) and passed it 15 min later; ventral fusion along the midline was then completed at about 240 min (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is stated as a temporal observation.

claim: Ventral fusion along the midline was completed at about 240 min after onset of germband extension.
source: The serosa approached the equator at the poles at about 150 min (Figure 3B) and passed it 15 min later; ventral fusion along the midline was then completed at about 240 min (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The closure rate during ventral fusion was about 11 µm/min along the anterior-to-posterior axis of the serosal window.
source: The increased resolution in ventral views allowed us to determine the specific dynamics of ventral fusion and suggested a closure rate of about 11 µm/min along the anterior-to-posterior axis of the serosal window, and 3 µm/min across (Figure 3F,G), which was considerably faster than rates that have been described for dorsal closure of the amnioserosa in D. melanogaster (Hutson et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figures 3F,G.

claim: The closure rate during ventral fusion was 3 µm/min across the serosal window.
source: The increased resolution in ventral views allowed us to determine the specific dynamics of ventral fusion and suggested a closure rate of about 11 µm/min along the anterior-to-posterior axis of the serosal window, and 3 µm/min across (Figure 3F,G), which was considerably faster than rates that have been described for dorsal closure of the amnioserosa in D. melanogaster (Hutson et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figures 3F,G.

claim: Ventral fusion in M. abdita was considerably faster than rates described for dorsal closure of the amnioserosa in D. melanogaster.
source: The increased resolution in ventral views allowed us to determine the specific dynamics of ventral fusion and suggested a closure rate of about 11 µm/min along the anterior-to-posterior axis of the serosal window, and 3 µm/min across (Figure 3F,G), which was considerably faster than rates that have been described for dorsal closure of the amnioserosa in D. melanogaster (Hutson et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with data from Hutson et al., 2003 and quantitative analysis shown in Figures 3F,G.

claim: M. abdita serosa spreading is a non-homogeneous process in which two periods of almost linear area growth are interrupted by a roughly 50-min interval without substantial tissue area increase.
source: Notably, our continuous mapping of area expansion indicated that M. abdita serosa spreading was a non-homogeneous process, in which two periods of almost linear area growth were interrupted by a roughly 50-min interval without substantial tissue area increase (70–120 min, Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: At the end of the interval without substantial tissue area increase, disjunction of the serosa from adjacent tissue was observed first at the anterior, then the posterior and finally at its lateral sides.
source: At the end of this interval, we observed disjunction of the serosa from adjacent tissue: first at the anterior, then the posterior and finally at its lateral sides (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Gene expression of Zen is reportedly high throughout stages in which tissue expansion paused.
source: For example, the interruption in serosa expansion could be explained by a temporal pause in a tissue-autonomous program of cell thinning and spreading. However, gene expression of the tissue-fate determining Hox-3 transcription factor Zen is reportedly high also throughout stages in which tissue expansion paused (Rafiqi et al., 2008), indicating little, if any, change in potential upstream genetic regulation of cell thinning and spreading.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rafiqi et al., 2008.

claim: High Zen expression throughout stages of paused tissue expansion indicates little, if any, change in potential upstream genetic regulation of cell thinning and spreading.
source: However, gene expression of the tissue-fate determining Hox-3 transcription factor Zen is reportedly high also throughout stages in which tissue expansion paused (Rafiqi et al., 2008), indicating little, if any, change in potential upstream genetic regulation of cell thinning and spreading.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation of high Zen expression and citation to Rafiqi et al., 2008.

claim: Mab-bsg is expressed in the yolk sac.
source: Analysis of Mab-bsg expression suggested that the gene was expressed in the yolk sac (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by expression analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Basigin is a trans-membrane protein that in D. melanogaster is enriched in the yolk sac membrane.
source: To generate a reporter that could visualize the yolk sac, we first cloned the M. abdita orthologue of basigin (Mab-bsg, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), which encodes a trans-membrane protein that in D. melanogaster is enriched in the yolk sac membrane (Reed et al., 2004; Goodwin et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Reed et al., 2004 and Goodwin et al., 2016.

claim: Fluorescent signals in serosa and yolk sac could be separated in time-lapse recordings along the dorsal midline.
source: Visual inspection of time-lapse recordings along the dorsal midline indicated that fluorescent signals in serosa and yolk sac could be separated, allowing us to distinguish between movements in either tissue (Figure 4A–C; Figure 4—video1).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figures 4A-C and Figure 4—video1.

claim: Optical flow analysis detected potential oscillations in membrane behavior along the anterior-to-posterior axis in the yolk sac.
source: With Basigin-eGFP established as reporter for the yolk sac membrane in M. abdita, we used its fluorescent signal to track movements at the yolk sac surface by optical flow (see Materials and methods). These analyses detected potential oscillations in membrane behavior along the anterior-to-posterior axis, which seemed to coincide with similar behavior in individual serosa cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by optical flow analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Oscillations in yolk sac membrane behavior seemed to coincide with similar behavior in individual serosa cells.
source: These analyses detected potential oscillations in membrane behavior along the anterior-to-posterior axis, which seemed to coincide with similar behavior in individual serosa cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by optical flow analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Direct comparison of general movements in yolk sac and serosa revealed a strong positive correlation.
source: The direct comparison of general movements in yolk sac and serosa revealed a strong positive correlation, which was very specific to individual serosa cells and the yolk sac membrane directly underneath (Figure 4E,F, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figures 4E,F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The positive correlation of movements between yolk sac and serosa was very specific to individual serosa cells and the yolk sac membrane directly underneath.
source: The direct comparison of general movements in yolk sac and serosa revealed a strong positive correlation, which was very specific to individual serosa cells and the yolk sac membrane directly underneath (Figure 4E,F, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figures 4E,F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Positive correlation of movements is indicative of strong mechanical coupling between yolk sac and extraembryonic tissue.
source: Such positive correlation of movements is indicative of strong mechanical coupling between yolk sac and extraembryonic tissue (Goodwin et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Goodwin et al., 2016.

claim: Coupling between yolk sac and serosa was significantly reduced after the second phase of serosa expansion had started.
source: We found coupling to be significantly reduced after the second phase of serosa expansion had started (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figures 4E,F.

claim: Yolk sac and serosa remained physically associated after coupling was reduced, but loosely enough to slide past each other.
source: Notably, coupling was not completely lost, suggesting that yolk sac and serosa remained physically associated, but loosely enough to slide past each other.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that coupling was not completely lost.

claim: Free spreading of the M. abdita serosa over the embryo was preceded by a decoupling of serosa and underlying yolk sac during paused tissue spreading.
source: Taken together, our results indicated that free spreading of the M. abdita serosa over the embryo was preceded by a decoupling of serosa and underlying yolk sac during paused tissue spreading (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the data presented, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mab-Mmp1 is expressed in yolk sac nuclei.
source: To test whether activity of this matrix metalloprotease was involved in mechanical decoupling of serosa and yolk sac, we cloned the M. abdita orthologue of Mmp1 (Mab-Mmp1) and found it expressed in yolk sac nuclei (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by expression analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Following knockdown of Mab-Mmp1 by RNAi, Mab-ddc expression was reduced to a dorsal domain in 96% of embryos (n = 100/104).
source: Following knockdown by RNAi (96%, n = 100/104) and CRISPR (56%, n = 77/136), Mab-ddc expression was reduced at corresponding stages to a dorsal domain, suggesting that serosa spreading was impaired (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data and observations shown in Figures 5C,D.

claim: Following knockdown of Mab-Mmp1 by CRISPR, Mab-ddc expression was reduced to a dorsal domain in 56% of embryos (n = 77/136).
source: Following knockdown by RNAi (96%, n = 100/104) and CRISPR (56%, n = 77/136), Mab-ddc expression was reduced at corresponding stages to a dorsal domain, suggesting that serosa spreading was impaired (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data and observations shown in Figures 5C,D.

claim: Reduction of Mab-ddc expression to a dorsal domain after Mab-Mmp1 knockdown suggests that serosa spreading was impaired.
source: Following knockdown by RNAi (96%, n = 100/104) and CRISPR (56%, n = 77/136), Mab-ddc expression was reduced at corresponding stages to a dorsal domain, suggesting that serosa spreading was impaired (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation of reduced Mab-ddc expression, shown in Figures 5C,D.

claim: In Mab-Mmp1 RNAi embryos corresponding to wildtype developmental stages prior to decoupling, the correlation of movements in serosa and yolk sac were comparable to wildtype.
source: In Mab-Mmp1 RNAi embryos corresponding to wildtype developmental stages prior to decoupling (90 – 120 min), the correlation of movements in serosa and yolk sac were comparable to wildtype and suggested mechanical coupling between the two membranes (Figure 5E,F; Figure 5—video1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figures 5E,F and Figure 5—video1.

claim: In Mab-Mmp1 RNAi embryos corresponding to wildtype developmental stages after decoupling, correlation of serosa and yolk sac movements remained virtually unchanged and were significantly higher than in wildtype.
source: In Mab-Mmp1 RNAi embryos corresponding to wildtype developmental stages after decoupling (140 – 200 min), correlation of serosa and yolk sac movements remained virtually unchanged and were significantly higher than in wildtype (Figure 5G,H; Figure 5—video1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figures 5G,H and Figure 5—video1.

claim: Mechanical coupling between serosa and yolk sac membranes was not broken up in Mab-Mmp1 RNAi embryos.
source: These results indicated that mechanical coupling between the two membranes was not broken up, thus explaining impaired serosa spreading.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the correlation data from Mab-Mmp1 RNAi embryos.

claim: In 9-hr old Mab-Mmp1 RNAi embryos, the serosa expanded to the mid-lateral side in 33% of embryos (n = 27/83).
source: In 9-hr old Mab-Mmp1 RNAi embryos, the serosa was not yet fused; in many embryos it expanded to the mid-lateral side (33%, n = 27/83), and a few embryos had strong phenotype with a dorsal serosa (4%, n = 3/83).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from analysis of fixed embryos.

claim: In 9-hr old Mab-Mmp1 RNAi embryos, 4% of embryos (n = 3/83) had strong phenotype with a dorsal serosa.
source: In 9-hr old Mab-Mmp1 RNAi embryos, the serosa was not yet fused; in many embryos it expanded to the mid-lateral side (33%, n = 27/83), and a few embryos had strong phenotype with a dorsal serosa (4%, n = 3/83).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from analysis of fixed embryos.

claim: In 11-hr old Mab-Mmp1 RNAi embryos, the serosa was fused in 77% of embryos (n = 30/39).
source: In 11-hr old Mab-Mmp1 RNAi embryos, the serosa was fused in most embryos (77%, n = 30/39), while a few specimen still showed the non-fused phenotype (23%, n = 9/39).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from analysis of fixed embryos.

claim: In 11-hr old Mab-Mmp1 RNAi embryos, 23% of embryos (n = 9/39) still showed the non-fused phenotype.
source: In 11-hr old Mab-Mmp1 RNAi embryos, the serosa was fused in most embryos (77%, n = 30/39), while a few specimen still showed the non-fused phenotype (23%, n = 9/39).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from analysis of fixed embryos.

claim: Serosa spreading was attenuated or delayed after knockdown of Mab-Mmp1.
source: These results suggested that serosa spreading was attenuated or delayed after knockdown of Mab-Mmp1.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the observation that serosa eventually fused in most embryos at later time points.

claim: Mab-Mmp1 may act redundantly with yet unknown factors to release the serosa from its yolk sac attachment.
source: To explain the observed delay in the completion of serosa closure, we cannot exclude a possibly incomplete knockdown of Mab-Mmp1 activity. However, we consider it more likely that Mab-Mmp1 acts redundantly with yet unknown factors to release the serosa from its yolk sac attachment.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the mechanism of serosa release.

claim: Tissue topology of the amnion in M. abdita is markedly different than the closed and ventral amnion that has been reported for non-cyclorrhaphan flies and most other insects.
source: Tissue topology of the amnion in M. abdita is thus markedly different than the closed and ventral amnion that has been reported for non-cyclorrhaphan flies and most other insects (Panfilio, 2008; Schmidt-Ott and Kwan, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Panfilio, 2008 and Schmidt-Ott and Kwan, 2016.

claim: The posterior amnion anlage in M. abdita is likely to reflect a more ancestral size.
source: While the posterior amnion anlage then is likely to reflect a more ancestral size and thus is still sufficient to form a vestigial ventral amnion, the lateral amnion is secondarily reduced (Kwan et al., 2016; Rafiqi et al., 2012), and the resulting tissue insufficient in area to close over the ventral side of the embryo proper.
evidence: The claim is an inference about evolutionary history, supported by citations to Kwan et al., 2016 and Rafiqi et al., 2012.

claim: The lateral amnion in M. abdita is secondarily reduced.
source: While the posterior amnion anlage then is likely to reflect a more ancestral size and thus is still sufficient to form a vestigial ventral amnion, the lateral amnion is secondarily reduced (Kwan et al., 2016; Rafiqi et al., 2012), and the resulting tissue insufficient in area to close over the ventral side of the embryo proper.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kwan et al., 2016 and Rafiqi et al., 2012.

claim: The comparatively fast fusion rate in the serosa can be explained by lack of segmental alignment and time consuming zippering as observed for dorsal closure in D. melanogaster.
source: Here we report that ventral closure of the serosa in M. abdita was substantially faster than dorsal closure of the D. melanogaster amnioserosa, and we propose that the comparatively fast fusion rate in the serosa can be explained by lack of segmental alignment and time consuming zippering as observed for dorsal closure in D. melanogaster (Jacinto et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is a proposed explanation based on comparison with D. melanogaster, supported by citation to Jacinto et al., 2002.

claim: Strong correlation of movements in serosa and yolk sac membranes indicated a tight coupling between the membranes in the phase of paused serosa spreading.
source: Strong correlation of movements in serosa and yolk sac membranes indicated a tight coupling between the membranes in the phase of paused serosa spreading, which could be observed until the extending germband reached about the middle of the egg.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the correlation analysis of movements.

claim: Tight coupling between serosa and yolk sac membranes could be observed until the extending germband reached about the middle of the egg.
source: Strong correlation of movements in serosa and yolk sac membranes indicated a tight coupling between the membranes in the phase of paused serosa spreading, which could be observed until the extending germband reached about the middle of the egg.
evidence: The claim is based on temporal observations of correlation.

claim: After the germband reached about the middle of the egg, correlation of movements between serosa and yolk sac was significantly reduced.
source: After that, correlation of movements between serosa and yolk sac was significantly reduced and disjunction of serosa and amnion could be observed.
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative analysis of correlation.

claim: Serosa disjunction was a gradual process that was first observed in the anterior and last in its lateral periphery.
source: Notably, serosa disjunction was a gradual process that was first observed in the anterior and last in its lateral periphery.
evidence: The claim is based on temporal and spatial observations of disjunction.

claim: Disjunction was characterized by a very steady and even expansion of the serosa leading edge without signs of tissue rupture.
source: Regardless of location and timing, disjunction was characterized by a very steady and even expansion of the serosa leading edge without signs of tissue rupture, suggesting that tissue-level decoupling from the yolk sac and cell-level loss of adhesion from the amnion had already occurred earlier.
evidence: The claim is based on observations of serosa behavior during disjunction.

claim: Tissue-level decoupling from the yolk sac and cell-level loss of adhesion from the amnion had already occurred before visible disjunction.
source: Regardless of location and timing, disjunction was characterized by a very steady and even expansion of the serosa leading edge without signs of tissue rupture, suggesting that tissue-level decoupling from the yolk sac and cell-level loss of adhesion from the amnion had already occurred earlier.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation of steady expansion without rupture.

claim: Coupling of serosa and yolk sac persisted in Mab-Mmp1 RNAi embryos substantially longer than in wildtype.
source: We found that coupling of serosa and yolk sac persisted in Mab-Mmp1 RNAi embryos substantially longer, and interactions between the two tissues remained comparable to that of wildtype embryos during paused serosa spreading.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of correlation data between wildtype and RNAi embryos.

claim: Free serosa spreading in M. abdita requires its decoupling from the yolk sac.
source: Taken together, our results strongly suggest that free serosa spreading in M. abdita requires its decoupling from the yolk sac.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the combined results from wildtype and Mab-Mmp1 RNAi embryos.

claim: Similar interactions between yolk sac and extraembryonic tissue have been reported in D. melanogaster at later stages of development.
source: Similar interactions between yolk sac and extraembryonic tissue have been reported previously in D. melanogaster, albeit at later stages of development, where they contribute to germband retraction and dorsal closure (Goodwin et al., 2016; Narasimha and Brown, 2004; Reed et al., 2004; Schöck and Perrimon, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Goodwin et al., 2016; Narasimha and Brown, 2004; Reed et al., 2004; and Schöck and Perrimon, 2003.

claim: Interactions of yolk sac and overlying epithelia have been long implicated in insect as well as vertebrate development.
source: More generally, interactions of yolk sac and overlying epithelia have been long implicated in insect as well as vertebrate development (Anderson, 1972a; Anderson, 1972b; Bruce, 2016; Counce, 1961; Schmidt-Ott and Kwan, 2016), suggesting that yolk sac-dependent regulation of serosa spreading in the M. abdita embryo may reflect a more common phenomenon.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Anderson, 1972a; Anderson, 1972b; Bruce, 2016; Counce, 1961; and Schmidt-Ott and Kwan, 2016.

claim: Yolk sac-dependent regulation of serosa spreading in the M. abdita embryo may reflect a more common phenomenon.
source: More generally, interactions of yolk sac and overlying epithelia have been long implicated in insect as well as vertebrate development (Anderson, 1972a; Anderson, 1972b; Bruce, 2016; Counce, 1961; Schmidt-Ott and Kwan, 2016), suggesting that yolk sac-dependent regulation of serosa spreading in the M. abdita embryo may reflect a more common phenomenon.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on comparative evidence from multiple species.

claim: The current model for the origin of the amnioserosa focuses on serosa differentiation by zen activity.
source: To explain the origin of the amnioserosa by such ancient genetic changes, the current model focuses on serosa differentiation by zen activity.
evidence: The claim describes the current model in the field.

claim: The current model stresses the absence of postgastrular zen activity in D. melanogaster.
source: It stresses the absence of postgastrular zen activity in D. melanogaster, outlines how terminal serosa differentiation is impaired as a consequence, and suggests that the resulting de-repression of amnion development has led to the formation of a non-spreading dorsal extraembryonic tissue (Rafiqi et al., 2008; Rafiqi et al., 2010; Schmidt-Ott and Kwan, 2016).
evidence: The claim describes the current model, supported by citations to Rafiqi et al., 2008; Rafiqi et al., 2010; and Schmidt-Ott and Kwan, 2016.

claim: According to the current model, de-repression of amnion development has led to the formation of a non-spreading dorsal extraembryonic tissue in D. melanogaster.
source: It stresses the absence of postgastrular zen activity in D. melanogaster, outlines how terminal serosa differentiation is impaired as a consequence, and suggests that the resulting de-repression of amnion development has led to the formation of a non-spreading dorsal extraembryonic tissue (Rafiqi et al., 2008; Rafiqi et al., 2010; Schmidt-Ott and Kwan, 2016).
evidence: The claim describes the current model, supported by citations to Rafiqi et al., 2008; Rafiqi et al., 2010; and Schmidt-Ott and Kwan, 2016.

claim: The amnioserosa may have alternatively originated by non-resolved tissue coupling between yolk sac and serosa.
source: Motivated by our results, and in the absence of a functionally described mechanism of postgastrular zen repression, we considered the possibility that the amnioserosa may have alternatively originated by non-resolved tissue coupling between yolk sac and serosa.
evidence: The claim is a speculative alternative hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Biomechanical and gene expression analyses in the amnioserosa support the idea that the amnioserosa has been, or still is, a composite tissue.
source: Topologically, and presumably also functionally, the resulting composite tissue of a non-spreading serosa and peripheral amnion would have shared similarities with the amnioserosa of D. melanogaster. Complementing biomechanical and gene expression analyses in the amnioserosa support the idea that the amnioserosa has been, or still is, a composite tissue (Gorfinkiel et al., 2009; Wada et al., 2007), and Mmp1 is not expressed in the yolk sac of D. melanogaster (Page-McCaw et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gorfinkiel et al., 2009 and Wada et al., 2007.

claim: Mmp1 is not expressed in the yolk sac of D. melanogaster.
source: Complementing biomechanical and gene expression analyses in the amnioserosa support the idea that the amnioserosa has been, or still is, a composite tissue (Gorfinkiel et al., 2009; Wada et al., 2007), and Mmp1 is not expressed in the yolk sac of D. melanogaster (Page-McCaw et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Page-McCaw et al., 2003.

claim: Development of injected M. abdita embryos was not notably affected by long-term SPIM imaging.
source: For all three landmarks, our live observations confirmed previously described timing (onset of germband extension 3:45 hr after egg laying (AEL), onset of germband retraction 8:10 hr AEL, end of germband retraction 11:05 hr AEL [Wotton et al., 2014]) within a window of 15 min (n = 24), which corresponded to the time interval of egg deposition. In our quantified SPIM recordings, we found the same timing of events, suggesting that development of injected M. abdita embryos was not notably affected by long-term SPIM imaging.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of developmental timing between live observations and SPIM recordings, with reference to Wotton et al., 2014.

claim: Extraembryonic tissues contribute to animal development, which often entails spreading over embryo or yolk.
source: Extraembryonic tissues contribute to animal development, which often entails spreading over embryo or yolk.
evidence: The claim is a general statement about extraembryonic tissue function.

claim: Apart from changes in cell shape, the requirements for extraembryonic tissue spreading are not well understood.
source: Apart from changes in cell shape, the requirements for this tissue spreading are not well understood.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Free serosa spreading is preceded by a prolonged pause in tissue expansion.
source: We describe the dynamics of this process in long-term, whole-embryo time-lapse recordings, demonstrating that free serosa spreading is preceded by a prolonged pause in tissue expansion.
evidence: The claim is a key finding from the time-lapse recordings described in the manuscript.

claim: The prolonged pause in tissue expansion reveals mechanical coupling to the underlying yolk sac, which is later released.
source: Closer examination of this pause reveals mechanical coupling to the underlying yolk sac, which is later released.
evidence: The claim is a key finding from the examination of the pause in tissue expansion.

claim: Mechanical coupling is prolonged after knockdown of M. abdita Matrix metalloprotease 1.
source: We find mechanical coupling prolonged and serosa spreading impaired after knockdown of M. abdita Matrix metalloprotease 1.
evidence: The claim is a key finding from the Mab-Mmp1 knockdown experiments.

claim: Serosa spreading is impaired after knockdown of M. abdita Matrix metalloprotease 1.
source: We find mechanical coupling prolonged and serosa spreading impaired after knockdown of M. abdita Matrix metalloprotease 1.
evidence: The claim is a key finding from the Mab-Mmp1 knockdown experiments.

claim: Tissue–tissue interactions provide a critical functional element to constrain spreading epithelia.
source: We conclude that tissue–tissue interactions provide a critical functional element to constrain spreading epithelia.
evidence: The claim is the main conclusion of the study.
